tldr: This paper redefines the collision avoidance metric not as traditional "distance" but as "adversarial time-to-collision (aTTC)"—the time until impact assuming the other agent takes worst-case evasive or pursuing maneuvers. By computing it rapidly via a neural network and embedding it into a control barrier function (CBF), the method halves the collision rate while up to doubling waypoint progress even in demanding 3D aerial environments with high-speed pursuers.
hero_caption: Overview of the 3D pursuit and collision avoidance scenarios evaluated in this paper: (a) independent-pursuit task where 8 friendly agents (blue) and 3 adversarial pursuers (red) navigate across a sphere; (b) formation-flight task navigating waypoints while maintaining a 90-degree chevron formation; (c) the intercept guidance law used by the pursuers.
overview:
Operating multiple drones or unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in shared airspace while reliably preventing collisions without stalling mission progress is a challenging problem. Conventional safety control approaches, such as control barrier functions (CBFs), have traditionally defined the safe set using Euclidean distance between agents. However, being close in space is safe if agents are moving apart, whereas being far apart is extremely dangerous if an agent is closing in at high speed. Distance-based checks fail to capture this difference in risk, leading to excessive slowdowns and detours that stall missions, or late interventions that cause collisions.

To tackle this, the authors conceived defining the barrier function directly in the temporal domain using time-to-collision (TTC). In automotive settings, TTC assumes constant-velocity straight-line motion; however, in open 3D space, the probability of point-mass agents colliding while holding constant velocity is virtually zero, causing traditional TTC to diverge to infinity. To solve this, they formulated an "adversarial TTC (aTTC)" representing the worst-case scenario where the peer maneuvers at maximum acceleration and top speed to intercept the ego agent. Furthermore, instead of solving heavy trajectory integrations online, they used a compact neural network surrogate with FiLM layers to provide a differentiable approximation of aTTC in sub-millisecond time, embedding it directly into a standard quadratic program (QP).

In extensive simulations spanning 50,000 seconds of flight time across two scenarios (independent pursuit and formation flight) using a 3D nonlinear aircraft model, aTTC-CBF halved the collision rate while achieving up to roughly double the waypoint progress compared to a higher-order distance-based CBF (HOCBF) baseline. The system demonstrated persistent, agile avoidance without breaking formation or sacrificing mission progress, even when adversaries were substantially faster than the ego aircraft.
contributions: Formulated adversarial time-to-collision (aTTC), a risk metric that assumes the peer agent applies its full maneuvering capability to cause a collision, stays finite in 3D space, and has a mathematical proof of finite-time reachability.
Showed that the barrier function based on aTTC has relative degree 1 with respect to the ego velocity, yielding an intuitive intercept-evasion gradient.

Enabled real-time (sub-millisecond) evaluation of aTTC and its gradient inside a QP across varying peer speed capabilities using a lightweight, differentiable neural network with Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM).

Statistically demonstrated lower collision rates, higher mission progress, and superior formation coherence compared to a conventional distance-based higher-order CBF baseline over long time-horizon 3D independent-pursuit and formation-flight simulations.

sections.heading: Why build a barrier in "time" instead of "distance"?
sections.summary: This section outlines the role of CBFs in multi-agent collision avoidance and highlights the limitations of existing approaches. To break away from the over-conservatism of distance-based metrics, the paper proposes a novel temporal barrier framework accounting for aircraft dynamics and adversarial intent.
sections.details:
In multi-agent collision avoidance, control barrier functions (CBFs) provide a powerful framework that guarantees forward invariance of a safe set (staying safe once inside) via linear inequality constraints inside a quadratic program (QP). However, most existing CBFs define safe boundaries based on Euclidean distance. This neglects velocity context—whether agents are closing in or flying apart—leading to either over-braking when situations are safe, or delayed intervention during rapid approaches.

While Velocity Obstacle-based CBFs (VO-CBF) have been explored, moving from 2D planar automotive settings to 3D aerial space with vertical maneuvers and independent acceleration makes anticipating future risk far more complex. Automotive TTC typically assumes "both agents continue on constant-velocity straight paths," but in expansive 3D space, the probability of small volumes colliding without maneuver is near zero, causing calculated TTC to blow up to infinity and rendering it useless as a control metric.

To overcome this, the authors conceived adversarial TTC (aTTC): "assuming the other agent uses its full dynamic envelope (maximum speed and acceleration) to collide as aggressively as possible, what is the minimum time to contact?" Just as human skiers or pedestrians intuitively rely on "reaction time" to evade obstacles, reframing collision risk into the time domain is the core starting point of this work.

sections.heading: Rigorous definition of adversarial TTC (aTTC) and its finiteness proof
sections.summary: Multi-agent systems are modeled as control-affine systems with bounded disturbances and actuation limits to formulate aTTC mathematically. Under the natural assumption that the peer agent's maximum speed exceeds the ego agent's current speed, the authors prove that aTTC is strictly bounded and finite in 3D space.
sections.details:
### 2.1 Problem Setting
Consider a multi-agent system composed of an ego vehicle (evader) and neighboring peers (pursuers or neutral agents). The state $x_i = (p_i, o_i)$ of agent $i$ comprises 3D position $p_i$ and internal variables $o_i$ such as attitude, governed by control-affine dynamics $\dot{x}_i = f_i(x_i) + g_i(x_i)u_i + w_i$ with control input $u_i$ and process noise $w_i$. Each agent has physical limits reflecting real aircraft: maximum speed $\bar{v}_i$ and maximum acceleration $\bar{a}_i$, and is modeled as a sphere of radius $r_{col}$. A collision is defined as the moment the inter-agent distance falls to $2r_{col}$ or below while closing in.

### 2.2 Adversarial TTC (aTTC) and Finiteness
While ego agent $i$ maintains its current velocity vector (zero acceleration, straight flight), peer $j$ seeks to bring the distance within $2r_{col}$ as quickly as possible within its admissible control inputs. The minimum time required for peer $j$ to achieve this is defined as aTTC ($\tau^*_{ij}$).

A key theoretical result is Proposition 2.2: Under the mild assumption that peer $j$'s top speed $\bar{v}_j$ strictly exceeds the instantaneous speed of ego agent $\lVert v_i \rVert$, and acceleration can be allocated in any direction, aTTC is guaranteed to have a finite upper bound from any initial configuration. The intuition behind the proof is straightforward: peer $j$ can first brake at maximum deceleration to come to a stop, then accelerate at maximum capability straight toward the projected path of the ego vehicle to intercept it. Because even this virtual, suboptimal pursuit strategy catches the ego agent in finite time, the optimal control infimum—aTTC—must also be finite. This yields a robust, non-diverging risk metric in 3D space.

sections.heading: Constructing temporal barriers and real-time computation via neural nets
sections.summary: Embedding aTTC directly into a CBF reveals the advantageous property of relative degree 1 with respect to velocity. To bypass the heavy online computational cost of exact reachable set calculations, proportional navigation (PN) pursuit is approximated using a FiLM-conditioned neural network surrogate running in under 1 ms inside a QP.
sections.details:
### 3.1 & 3.2 Control Barrier Functions via aTTC
The safe set is defined as $h_{ij}(\mathbf{x}) = \tau^*_{ij} - \tau_c \geq 0$, where $\tau_c > 0$ represents a safety threshold in seconds corresponding to controller or pilot reaction time. While conventional distance-based CBFs have relative degree 2 with respect to acceleration inputs—requiring cumbersome higher-order CBF (HOCBF) designs—aTTC directly yields relative degree 1 when ego velocity is a state variable (Proposition 3.4, Corollary 3.5). Moreover, its gradient $\nabla_{v_i} \tau^*_{ij}$ aligns parallel to the incoming intercept vector, scaling inversely with closing velocity to steer the aircraft away from the collision course. This behavior is both physically intuitive and mathematically elegant.

### 3.3 & 3.4 Pursuit Law Fixing and Neural Network Surrogate
However, computing exact aTTC online requires dynamic reachable sets, which is computationally prohibitive. As a practical solution, the authors fixed the peer's behavior to a standard intercept strategy—Proportional Navigation (PN)—defining a pursuit-law TTC $\tau^P_{ij}$, which preserves the desirable relative-degree-1 property.

To compute this forward trajectory integration within milliseconds, they introduced a neural network surrogate $G_\theta(\Delta p_{ij}, v_i, v_j; \bar{v}_j)$. To flexibly handle varying peer dynamic limits (top speed $\bar{v}_j$), the architecture incorporates Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM), where intermediate layers are scaled and shifted by a conditioning network. This enables instantaneous, analytical evaluation of both time-to-collision and its state gradients, allowing direct incorporation into standard CBF quadratic programs (CBF-QP).

sections.heading: Unmatched avoidance performance verified in demanding 3D simulations
sections.summary: Extensive simulations spanning 50,000 seconds were conducted across independent pursuit and formation flight using a 3D Dubins aircraft model with stochastic wind disturbances. Compared to a distance-based HOCBF, the proposed method drastically reduced collisions, doubled waypoint progress, and preserved tight formation coherence.
sections.details:
### 4.1 & 4.2 Experimental Setup and Surrogate Accuracy
The aircraft dynamics were modeled using a 3D Dubins model with bounded roll/pitch angular rates and thrust acceleration, subjected to Wiener process stochastic disturbances (wind). The surrogate network was trained on 10 million offline trajectory samples. As shown in Figure F1, in the critical danger zone where $\tau^* < 30$ s, the mean absolute error (MAE) is under 1.5 seconds. Crucially, the error distribution exhibits negative skewness, meaning the network systematically errs on the conservative side by predicting slightly earlier collisions—a highly desirable property for safety control.

### 4.4 Independent Multi-Agent Collision Avoidance
Eight ego agents navigated toward reciprocal waypoints on a 3.75 km radius sphere, amidst up to 3 adversarial pursuers in a congested volume.
- No adversaries: aTTC-CBF suffered only about one-third of the collisions experienced by HOCBF, while achieving roughly 3 times the waypoint progress (approaching nominal unconstrained flight speeds).
- Slower adversaries (speed ratio 0.9): aTTC-CBF cut the collision rate by more than half compared to HOCBF, with 1.8 times greater progress.
- Faster adversaries (speed ratio 1.5): In this extreme regime, HOCBF panicked, driving mission progress down to 30% of nominal. In contrast, aTTC-CBF maintained 58% progress while keeping the collision rate at half that of HOCBF.

Examining the mission volume occupancy in Figure F3 (distance distribution from the origin), HOCBF was pushed far outside the task arena by fleeing pursuers, whereas aTTC-CBF remained compact inside the operational zone. Figure F4 reveals that during near-miss encounters, aTTC-CBF commanded control inputs up to maximum angular rate limits to execute sharp turns, escaping faster pursuers with ~50% probability where HOCBF escaped in only 5% of cases.

### 4.5 Evasive Maneuvers During Formation Flight
In an 8-agent 90-degree chevron formation flight scenario, pursuers targeted formation members. Under HOCBF, targeted agents were pushed far out of rank, nearly doubling average formation tracking errors and causing the formation to collapse. In contrast, as shown in Figure F5, aTTC-CBF preserved tight formation coherence; targeted aircraft performed minimal evasive maneuvers and promptly returned to their assigned slots.

While distance-based HOCBF (red) gets pushed far outward as pursuer speed increases, aTTC-CBF (blue) remains within a compact operational volume even against faster adversaries (square markers).

sections.heading: Summary and future directions
sections.summary: This section synthesizes the effectiveness of evaluating collision risk in the time domain via aTTC-CBF, reinforcing its advantages over geometric distance methods. It also discusses avenues for addressing peer intent uncertainty and establishing formal surrogate guarantees.
sections.details:
This paper introduced aTTC-CBF, capturing aircraft collision risk through the natural metric of time. Grounding risk in aircraft dynamics and opponent maneuvering limits allows sharp, context-aware interventions: safe proximity is permitted when separating, while early avoidance triggers when on an intercept vector. This eliminates excessive conservatism and enables aggressive yet safe autonomous flight.

Three directions were highlighted for future work:
- Diverse agent intent: Moving beyond single worst-case or PN assumptions toward frameworks that incorporate belief distributions over cooperative and adversarial intents.
- Unknown peer dynamics: Developing online estimation and learning routines to handle peers whose kinematic or dynamic limits are not known a priori.
- Theoretical safety with surrogates: Formulating hybrid fallback strategies—such as switching to conservative analytical barriers in high-uncertainty regions—to provide formal safety guarantees despite neural network approximation errors.

sections.heading: Appendix: Tailoring the surrogate NN with a danger-weighted Huber loss
sections.summary: This section details the custom loss formulation used to train the surrogate network, focusing model capacity on the safety-critical low-TTC regime.
sections.details:
To train the surrogate network, the authors adopted a weighted Huber loss inversely proportional to time-to-collision $\tau^*$, rather than standard mean squared error (MSE):

$$L = \frac{1}{\tau^{*n}} \operatorname{Huber}(\hat{\tau} - \tau^*)$$

Empirically, an exponent of $n=3$ achieved the best performance. Standard MSE or unweighted losses struggle because safe multi-agent encounters produce millions of samples with very large $\tau^*$ (negligible risk), which drown out gradient updates for the rare, critical low-$\tau^*$ samples where immediate evasion is vital. Setting a Huber threshold of $\delta = 1$ s ensures smooth gradients near zero while preventing extreme prediction outliers from destabilizing training.

takeaways: In 3D multi-agent collision avoidance, distance-based thresholds cause excessive slowing and mission stalls; defining barrier functions via adversarial time-to-collision (aTTC) overcomes this conservatism.

An aTTC barrier function naturally exhibits relative degree 1 with respect to aircraft acceleration inputs, generating an intuitive avoidance gradient along the intercept vector without needing higher-order CBF formulations.

Heavy optimal control and trajectory integrations can be approximated using a compact FiLM-conditioned neural network surrogate, executing in under 1 ms in a differentiable form suitable for real-time QPs.

Training surrogate networks with loss functions weighted inversely by TTC focuses accuracy on the safety-critical danger zone, producing conservative, control-friendly models biased toward safe predictions.
limitations: Assumes peer agents follow proportional navigation (PN) guidance or known dynamic bounds; theoretical safety guarantees are limited against adversaries with unmodeled intents or unknown flight dynamics.
Because the neural network surrogate exhibits small approximation errors, strict forward invariance (zero probability of collision) cannot be mathematically guaranteed.
Under severe actuator saturation (e.g., maximum acceleration limits) or strong persistent disturbances, the quadratic program (QP) safety constraints may become infeasible.
